1:
The psalm bears the plainest of headings, "To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David," yet opens not in praise but in a cry wrung from a soul that feels abandoned, and the witnesses gather first about the occasion and then about the ache of the words. The reformed John Calvin sets the scene: David, weighed down by a long succession of calamities, implores the only aid left him, and at the last, taking courage, holds fast the assured hope of life even amid the terrors of death. The complaint of being forgotten, Calvin insists, is no failure of faith but its very exercise, for to own in affliction that God still cares for us is not nature's way; though it seemed to David he was forsaken, the eyes of his mind, guided by faith's light, penetrated even to the grace of God hidden in darkness. His fellow reformed voice John Gill reads "how long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever?" as the language of a people who, when God delays deliverance and withholds the tokens of his love, conclude in their own apprehension that they are forgotten — though God can no more forget the children for whom a book of remembrance is written than oblivion can fall on him at all.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch hear a shape as much as a sound: three strophes of decreasing magnitude, a long deep sigh, then a gentler prayer, and then the joy that anticipates its answer, the song casting up ever-lessening waves until it grows still as a mirror-smooth sea. They set the trouble, with Hitzig, in the days when Saul posted watchers to hunt David from place to place; yet the season is not agreed, for Calvin records the opinion of those who referred the psalm rather to Absalom's conspiracy, while Clarke reports the supposition that it was written far later, in the captivity, as Israel's prayer worn out with bondage. Ellicott, the other grammatical-historical witness, judges the double question of the Authorized Version unnecessary, and, noting with Renan how the poet seems to have begun on one plan and finished on another, would render simply, "how long wilt thou continue to forget me?" The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke marks that the little Hebrew phrase for "how long" is sounded four times over these first two verses, a token of deep dejection and extreme earnestness, and takes "hide thy face" for the withdrawal of any clear sense of God's approbation.

The puritan-evangelical voices feel the wound most personally. Matthew Henry owns that David construed God's delay as unkindness — as though God had forgotten his promises, his covenant, his former lovingkindness — and calls it a peevish expression of prevailing fear that a good man's second thought will retract; yet herein, Henry adds, David was a type of Christ upon the cross, crying, "My God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Charles Spurgeon turns the fourfold "How long?" over and over, hearing desire mingled with an impatience hard to keep from murmuring, then checks the complaint at its root: "Can God forget? Can Omniscience fail in memory?" — recalling Zion's like despondency, "my Lord hath forgotten me" (Isa. 49:14). The latin-fathers voice reads the heading itself as mystery: Augustine takes "unto the end" for Christ, who is the end of the law, and hears "how long wilt Thou forget me unto the end?" as the soul's longing to understand Christ, the Wisdom of God and end of all its aim. The witnesses do not divide over the ache: the words are faith's complaint, not unbelief's — the groan of a man who prays even while he fears he is forgotten.
2:
The lament's second stroke turns from God's seeming absence to the turmoil it breeds within, and the witnesses work at the strange phrase "how long shall I take counsel in my soul." The reformed John Gill sets aside the good sense of taking counsel — of God, or of faithful friends — and hears instead a man at his wits' end, cast about in his mind, framing device after device yet knowing no way to take nor course to steer; the phrase denotes not wise deliberation but the anxiety of one left to be his own and only counsellor. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it much the same: the soul continually frames ways and means of deliverance, and they all come to naught, as a conscience feeling the burden of sin tries innumerable schemes of self-recovery, none of which can speak it peace; and "mine enemy be exalted" he refers to Satan, who seems to triumph while the soul lies under the curse of a broken law. John Wesley compresses the whole to a sigh: "how long shall I be in such perplexities, not knowing what course to take?"

The grammatical-historical witnesses press the Hebrew harder, and here a real difference opens. Keil and Delitzsch keep the plain sense, setting the "sorrow in my heart daily" over against a God who seems to know nothing of his servant's need. But Charles Ellicott doubts whether the word for "soul" can stand for the mind at all, and, rendering the line literally "put plans unto my soul," would translate "how long shall I form plans against my soul, having sorrow in my heart all the day?" — finding in it, and in the "sleep of death" of the next verse (v.3), the suspicion that suicide had entered the psalmist's thoughts. So the witnesses divide over what counsel it is that David takes: the frustrated devices of a man in perplexity, as Gill, Clarke, and Wesley have it, or, as Ellicott reads it, the dark plans a despairing soul lays against its own life.

The latin-fathers voice hears something else again. Augustine takes "how long shall I place counsel in my soul" as an answer to the opening cry: so long, O Lord, wilt Thou forget me and turn away Thy face, until I place counsel in my own soul to work mercy perfectly; there is no need of counsel, he observes, but in adversity, so that the question amounts to asking, how long shall I be in adversity? The "sorrow in my heart through the day" he takes for continuance, day standing for the whole stretch of time from which each soul longs to be free, that it may rise to things eternal and not endure man's day. The witnesses do not finally divide over the grief; they agree that the inward counsel is a burden and not a comfort, whether it be the vain projecting of a hunted man, the self-destroying thought of a despairing one, or the soul's long ache to be done with the counsels of adversity altogether.
3:
With the third verse the complaint breaks into open petition, and the witnesses mark how the very form of the prayer — "consider and hear me, O LORD my God" — leans upon the covenant bond it names. The reformed John Gill hears David rightly applying to God amid all his distress, claiming an interest that darkness and desertion had not cancelled, and begging God to "consider" his affliction, his many and mighty enemies, and his own weakness, to look on him with pity, and to "hear" him so as to answer, and answer at once. The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon feels the prayer lift its voice like a watchman proclaiming daybreak: the mercy-seat is the life of hope and the death of despair, and the cry "O Lord my God!" is a glorious fact, that our interest in our God is not destroyed by all our trials, for we may lose our gourds but not our God, the title-deed of heaven being written not in sand but in eternal brass.

Over "lighten mine eyes" the witnesses spread the phrase into its several senses. Spurgeon takes it of the eye of faith made clear to see God in the dark, the eye of watchfulness kept open against the snare, and the eye of the understanding illuminated, with perhaps an allusion to that cheering of the spirits which brightens the face and makes the eyes to sparkle. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read it as the imparting of new life (Ezra 9:8), the fresh clear brightness of the eye that answers to the light of love beaming from the divine countenance, the very opposite of eyes dimmed with sorrow and ready to break (1 Sam. 14:27). The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps it plain — "revive and comfort, and deliver me from the darkness of death, which is ready to come upon me."

The closing dread, "lest I sleep the sleep of death," the witnesses take literally and gravely. Charles Ellicott renders it "give light to my eyes that I may not go to sleep in death," that is, sleep and never wake, the "sleep unto death" of the Septuagint (Ps. 6:5). The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke will not soften "consider and hear me" but presses it to "answer me": I have prayed, I am seeking thy face, I am lost without thee, I am in darkness, my life draws nigh to destruction, and if I die unforgiven I die eternally — O Lord my God, consider this, hear and answer, for thy name's sake. The witnesses do not divide; they hear in the verse the pivot of the psalm, the moment when the long "how long" of complaint turns itself into a definite plea, and a man on the brink of the sleep of death asks the God he still calls his own to open his eyes before they close for ever.
4:
The petition of the previous verse now names its motive, and the witnesses hear David plead the honour of God against the boast of the foe — "lest mine enemy say, I have prevailed against him." The reformed John Gill marks this as an argument that God himself takes notice of, and for whose sake he does not give up his people into their enemies' hands; and he records the Chaldee paraphrase, which turns the "enemy" inward, making it the evil imagination or corruption of nature personified, as the apostle personifies indwelling sin, prevailing when it pushes to evil and hinders good, or else applying the word to Satan, the great enemy who triumphs whenever his temptation succeeds. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke follows the same inward track: Satan's ordinary method is to urge strongly to sin, to blind the understanding and inflame the passions, and when he succeeds he triumphs by insults and reproaches, none so ready then as he to tell the poor soul how deeply and ungratefully it has sinned; and "when I am moved," Clarke says, means when moved from one's steadfastness and overcome, so that he cries out over the desolation wrought by the fall of a righteous soul — infidels filled with scoffing, the Church clad in mourning, the Spirit grieved.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keeps the enemy nearer to hand, hearing David dread that Saul, or Satan, should be gratified in his fall: the enemy would say, "So would I have it," and the troublers would "rejoice when I am moved," pleased in his grief and promising themselves a complete victory. Henry reads this as David's care for God's honour more than his own, since to let the wicked thus trample on all that is sacred in heaven and earth would seem to reflect dishonour upon God's power and promise.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the verse at the hinge of the psalm's turn, where the five lines of lament and four of prayer give way to the three of joyous anticipation: by the emphatic "but I" of the next breath David sets himself in opposition to his foes, who desire his death, while he casts himself upon the mercy of God. The witnesses do not divide over the danger; whether the enemy be Saul at the mouth of the cave or Satan at the door of the heart, they agree that David's dread is not for his life only but for the credit of the God whose servant he is, and that he makes the enemy's very insolence a plea to move the God who will not see his own put to open shame.
5:
"But I have trusted in thy mercy" — with the little adversative the whole psalm turns, and the witnesses feel the sudden calm break over it. The reformed John Gill traces the ascent step by step: the psalmist's faith and comfort grew by prayer, so that from complaining he passed to praying and from praying to believing, trusting not in himself, nor in his own righteousness and merits, but in the mercy of God — and not the bare absolute mercy of God, but that grace and goodness displayed in the plenteous redemption which is by Christ, a sufficient ground of faith and hope. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marvels at the change wrought in so few lines: at the opening David is drooping, trembling, ready to sink into despair, and at the close rejoicing and enlarged in praise. God's mercy, Henry says, is the support of his faith — "finding I have that to trust to, I am comforted, though I have no merit of my own" — for in former distresses he had trusted that mercy and never found it fail, so that even when God hid his face, and without were fightings and within were fears, his confidence in mercy was as an anchor in a storm, by which, though tossed, he was not overset; and that faith in mercy filled his heart with joy in salvation, since joy and peace come by believing (Rom. 15:13).

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears the same trust as a plea against falling: thou wilt not suffer me to fall, or if I have fallen, wilt thou not once more lift up the light of thy countenance upon me and cover my sin? And "my heart shall rejoice in thy salvation" he weighs with care, for there is no true joy but of the heart, and the heart cannot rejoice till all guilt is taken away from the conscience.

The grammatical-historical witnesses attend to the rhythm and the wording of the peace. Charles Ellicott reads the emphatic "but as for me," and hears in the very cadence of the Hebrew the restfulness that has taken the place of the opening despair — "it hath a dying fall"; and he notes that the Septuagint and Vulgate carry an added clause, found in no manuscript, "yea, I will praise the name of the Lord most high." Keil and Delitzsch fix the theology of the verbs: "trusted" denotes faith as clinging fast to God, and the voluntative "my heart shall rejoice" presupposes the sure realisation of the hope, the joy already certain of the deliverance that will turn and terminate his affliction. The witnesses do not divide; they hear in the verse the storm-tossed soul come suddenly to harbour, the man who began by crying "how long" now resting his whole cause, without reserve, on the mercy and salvation of his God.
6:
The psalm that opened in the dark of "how long" closes in the light of a vow to sing, and the witnesses gather to hear the complaint resolved wholly into praise — "I will sing unto the LORD, because he hath dealt bountifully with me." The reformed John Gill reads the song as the fruit of the believing that went before: in prayer faith is encouraged, and through believing the heart is filled with a joy that the lips must express in songs of praise, ascribing the glory of salvation to the Lord and giving him thanks for every mercy and blessing of life. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke dwells on the bounty and the joy together. That heart is turned to God's praise, he says, which has a clear sense of God's favour; and the Hebrew "he hath dealt bountifully" he renders "he hath recompensed me" — my sorrows were deep and long, but in thy favour is life, and a moment of this spiritual joy is worth a year of sorrow, for God has given the oil of joy for the spirit of heaviness and the garments of praise for mourning. Clarke lingers, too, over an old manuscript Psalter in the Scottish tongue, whose author he takes for no mere commentator but a truly religious man acquainted with the travail of the soul, and finds in its ancient words the proof that the language of true Christian experience has been one in all times and nations.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the closing note as the resolution of the whole song's music. The perfect tense, "he hath dealt bountifully," they understand of a celebration that follows the fact which inspires it (Ps. 116:7), so that with the two quiet iambics of the last words the song sinks to rest: though it rage without as much now as ever, peace reigns in the depth of the storm-tossed soul, now grown as calm as the sea when smooth as a mirror. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley accounts for that past tense another way, for it is a common thing, he says, for David and the other prophets to speak of future deliverances as if they were already come, both to signify the infallible certainty of the thing and to voice their firm assurance of it; and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads it so too, hearing David speak of the salvation as a thing already past because by faith he had received its earnest and was as confident of it as if it had been done.

The witnesses do not divide; they close the psalm where its whole movement has been tending, on the strange and blessed spectacle of a man who began by asking whether God had forgotten him for ever and ends by singing, as of a thing already done, that God has dealt bountifully with him — the lament tuned, before the last line is sung, into a song of praise.
